question.what: A profitability map of the product portfolio: for each product line, revenue and gross margin over the trailing four quarters, plus the trend against the prior four.
question.why: It answers the first board question about any portfolio — which lines pay for the company and which are being carried — and is the factual basis for investment and divestment arguments.

totals-stat.label: Portfolio totals
totals-stat.what: The whole-portfolio headline over the trailing four quarters: total revenue, total gross margin, and how much of that margin the flagship lines contribute.
totals-stat.why: The concentration of margin in one or two lines is the risk headline: if most of the profit engine is a single franchise, everything else rides on it.

gm-by-line.what: Each product line's revenue next to the gross margin it kept, over the same trailing four quarters.
gm-by-line.why: Revenue and margin rank lines differently — a big-revenue line with thin margin funds less than it appears to. This is where that gap becomes visible.
gm-by-line.how_to_read: For each line, compare the two bars: the wider the gap between revenue and margin, the more of that line's sales are eaten by direct costs.

gm-share.what: Each line's slice of total portfolio gross margin — margin dollars restated as shares of the whole.
gm-share.why: This is the "who funds the company" chart in one view; a line with a small slice consumes management attention disproportionate to what it contributes.

gm-trend.what: Each line's gross-margin percentage in the most recent four quarters, next to the same figure for the four quarters before that.
gm-trend.why: Direction matters as much as level: a healthy-margin line that is eroding is a different decision than a thin-margin line that is improving.
gm-trend.how_to_read: For each line, if the recent bar is below the prior bar, margin is eroding.

revenue-trend.what: Quarterly revenue over time for the largest lines, with the smaller lines combined into one "other" series to keep the chart readable.
revenue-trend.why: It shows whether the portfolio's growth is broad or riding a single line, and when any line's trajectory changed.

opex-by-line.what: Operating expense (R&D, sales, overhead) split by product line — data the finance system does not currently track at line level, so the chart states the gap instead of estimating it.
opex-by-line.why: Gross margin alone can flatter a line that quietly consumes disproportionate engineering and support effort. Until opex is attributable by line, "which lines consume the company" is only half-answered.

terms.definition: Revenue minus the direct cost of producing and delivering the product — what is left to fund R&D, sales, and overhead. A product line can post healthy revenue and still consume the company if its margin is thin.

questions.question: How concentrated are we — PCA franchise, top-3 GPOs, single systems — and what does losing one anchor GPO do to the 5-year plan?
questions.verdict_headline: Meridian Health Alliance carries 38.4% of FY2025 direct-book revenue — above the 30% guardrail on the direct-book basis, and basis-sensitive: the direct book covers 50.6% of total FY2025 revenue, and Meridian Health Alliance's floor share of TOTAL revenue is 19.4% (under the guardrail); top-3 accounts 25.5%, PCA franchise 74.5%; losing the anchor GPO dents every plan year by $15.6M (14.9% of the FY2026 plan) under the stated constant-dent scenario

question.what: A concentration analysis: how much of revenue depends on a single buying group (GPO), the top few accounts, and the PCA product franchise — and what losing the anchor buying group would do to the five-year plan.
question.why: Concentration is the classic hidden fragility: strong totals can sit on one contract or one franchise. Boards use this to judge whether the plan survives losing its biggest dependency.

concentration-stat.label: Concentration headline
concentration-stat.what: The three concentration measures in one place: the largest GPO's share of directly tracked revenue, the top accounts' combined share, and the PCA franchise's share.
concentration-stat.why: Each is a separate way the business could be hurt by a single event — one contract loss, one account loss, or one franchise-level disruption.

share-by-gpo.what: Directly tracked revenue split by the buying group (GPO) each account purchases through.
share-by-gpo.why: A GPO relationship is a single commercial decision covering many hospitals; the bigger one GPO's bar, the more revenue moves on that one decision.

top-accounts.what: The largest individual customer accounts by directly tracked revenue.
top-accounts.why: Account-level concentration is the most concrete form of dependency — these are the named customers whose renewals matter most.

franchise-share.what: Directly tracked revenue cut by product franchise — how much rides on the PCA family (including the subscription software that sells on top of it) versus everything else.
franchise-share.why: Franchise concentration means a single clinical or safety event in that category can touch most of the revenue at once.

basis-sensitivity.what: The same concentration measure computed on two different denominators: the directly tracked ("direct book") revenue versus total company revenue.
basis-sensitivity.why: The direct book covers only part of total revenue, so a concentration verdict can flip depending on which base is used. Showing both keeps the conclusion honest about what the data can and cannot say.
basis-sensitivity.how_to_read: If the two bars straddle the guardrail line, the verdict is basis-dependent — treat it as unresolved rather than passed or failed.

gpo-share-trend.what: Each major GPO's share of directly tracked revenue across fiscal years.
gpo-share-trend.why: Whether concentration is building or unwinding matters more than any single year's level.

plan-loss-scenario.what: The revenue plan of record next to a modeled scenario in which the anchor GPO's revenue is removed.
plan-loss-scenario.why: This is the "what does losing our biggest dependency actually cost" line — the gap between the two curves is the size of the bet on that relationship.

verdict.what: The verdict tests the largest GPO's share against a concentration guardrail — a maximum share of revenue any single buying group should carry. The guardrail here is a stand-in, not a board-adopted limit.
verdict.why: Until the board adopts a real limit, a breach is a conversation-starter, not a policy violation — but the exposure it flags is real either way.

terms.definition: Group Purchasing Organization — a buying intermediary that negotiates supply contracts on behalf of many hospitals at once. One GPO agreement can control purchasing access to dozens of hospital systems, which is why revenue concentrated in a single GPO is a board-level risk.

Integrated Delivery Network — a health system that operates multiple hospitals and care sites under one ownership and, typically, one purchasing decision. One IDN decision can switch every pump across the network.

Patient-Controlled Analgesia — pain-medication (typically opioid) infusion where the patient presses a button to receive a dose, within programmed safety limits. The device class of our lead product, PP3500.

questions.question: What share of revenue is recurring today vs the Y5 plan — and which parts of the $350M target are contracted, modeled, or aspiration?
questions.verdict_headline: Recurring revenue is 10.8% of revenue today (FY2026H1) vs 68.6% planned for FY2030; of the $350.0M target, $128.0M rides on already-cleared products, $12.0M on letter-to-file changes, and $210.0M (60.0%) sits behind FDA decisions not yet received — and within the $240.0M recurring proxy itself, $210.0M (87.5%) is behind those decisions

question.what: A decomposition of the long-range revenue target: how much revenue is recurring today versus planned, and how much of the plan is contracted, modeled, or aspiration — including how much waits on FDA decisions.
question.why: A headline target means little until you know what it is made of. This separates the parts that are already earned or committed from the parts that are still a bet, so the board can judge the plan's real risk.

recurring-stat.label: Recurring share — today vs plan
recurring-stat.what: The share of revenue that is recurring (subscriptions) today, the share the final plan year assumes, and how much of the target sits behind FDA decisions not yet received.
recurring-stat.why: The distance between today's recurring share and the plan's is the transformation the company is betting on; the FDA-dependent slice is the part of that bet the company does not fully control.

recurring-share-trend.what: The recurring share of revenue over time — actuals against the trajectory the plan assumes.
recurring-share-trend.why: If actuals are not bending toward the planned curve, the end-state recurring mix is drifting from plan years before the target date arrives.

plan-by-bucket.what: Planned revenue per plan year, split into evidence buckets: contracted (signed), modeled (projected from current run-rates by a stated method), and aspiration (targets without a mechanism yet).
plan-by-bucket.why: Watching the bucket mix across years shows when the plan shifts from earned revenue to hoped-for revenue — usually the later years.

y5-decomposition.what: The final-year revenue target broken into the same contracted / modeled / aspiration buckets.
y5-decomposition.why: This is the honest anatomy of the headline number: the aspiration slice is the part with no mechanism behind it yet.

y5-recurring-decomposition.what: The recurring (subscription) portion of the final-year target, broken into the same evidence buckets.
y5-recurring-decomposition.why: The recurring transformation is the plan's centerpiece, so it deserves its own anatomy — a recurring target that is mostly aspiration is a strategy, not a forecast.

terms.definition: Revenue that repeats without a new sale — subscriptions and service contracts — as opposed to one-time hardware purchases. It is valued for predictability, which is why the share of revenue that is recurring is tracked against plan.

A documented internal decision that a device change is minor enough not to need a new FDA submission. The rationale is recorded in the company's own files and the product stays on the market — so revenue behind letter-to-file changes is not waiting on FDA.

The standard FDA review route for most moderate-risk devices. The maker shows its new device is as safe and effective as a similar device already legally on the market, and FDA "clears" it for sale. Clearance records are public, so competitor clearances show what rivals are now allowed to sell — and how fast they got there.

Predetermined Change Control Plan — a plan, authorized by FDA in advance, that lets a company make specified future changes to a cleared device (especially software) without filing a new submission each time. Revenue that depends on a PCCP still needs FDA to authorize that plan first.

questions.question: Does the subscription model work at unit level — LTV per connected pump vs cost-to-serve, and is Cloud Suite cannibalizing hardware ASP?
questions.verdict_headline: Unit economics fail the guardrail: LTV per connected pump $2,237 vs $2,720 cost-to-serve over the same 5-year horizon (ratio 0.82 vs the 3.0 floor); 28 of 39 active sites run ARR below cost-to-serve — concentrated in small sites — and the mean hardware discount at subscribed sites is 5.8% vs the 5% tolerance

question.what: Unit economics of the subscription: what one connected pump's subscription earns over the horizon (LTV) versus what it costs to serve, and whether subscription deals are being bought with hardware discounts.
question.why: A subscription business that loses money per unit gets worse as it grows. This is the check that the razor-and-blades model actually works at the level of a single pump.

unit-econ-stat.label: LTV vs cost-to-serve
unit-econ-stat.what: The three-number unit-economics headline: revenue expected per connected pump over the horizon, the cost to serve it over the same horizon, and their ratio.
unit-econ-stat.why: The ratio is the whole business model in one number — below 1.0 each connected pump loses money; a healthy subscription business clears its cost several times over.
unit-econ-stat.how_to_read: Higher is better. Compare the ratio against the floor the expectation sets; the floor itself is a standard industry heuristic, not an underwritten target.

band-economics.what: Subscription revenue versus cost-to-serve per pump, split by site size (small, mid, large fleets).
band-economics.why: Fixed per-site costs spread across few pumps can make small sites structurally unprofitable — this shows whether the losses concentrate in a site profile rather than being uniform.

discount-by-band.what: The average hardware discount granted, split by the same site-size bands.
discount-by-band.why: If subscribed sites systematically get deeper hardware discounts, the subscription revenue is partly a transfer from hardware, not new money.

discount-sensitivity.what: How the hardware-discount finding moves under alternative readings — testing whether an apparent breach is real or within sampling noise.
discount-sensitivity.why: A threshold miss driven by a handful of deals should trigger a different response than a systematic pattern; this chart separates the two.

attach-gap.what: Sites whose pumps are connected (hardware capable) but carry no subscription.
attach-gap.why: These are the cheapest growth available — the hardware cost is already sunk, so converting them is nearly pure subscription margin.

arr-build.what: How annual recurring revenue accumulated as sites activated, built from each active site's start date. Sites that later churned are not represented, so the curve is survivor-biased.
arr-build.why: The build curve shows whether subscription momentum is accelerating or flattening — with the stated caveat that it flatters by construction.

econ-history.what: The LTV-to-cost-to-serve ratio tracked across successive analyses — history that will only exist once this analysis has been recomputed over multiple periods.
econ-history.why: The trajectory of unit economics matters more than any single reading; the chart states the gap rather than faking a trend from one point.

verdict.what: The verdict compares per-pump subscription economics against a minimum-ratio guardrail and checks whether hardware discounts at subscribed sites exceed tolerance.
verdict.why: Together the two checks answer "does the subscription make money, and is it cannibalizing the hardware business to do it?"

terms.definition: Lifetime Value — the total revenue expected from one customer (here, one connected pump's subscription) over the analysis horizon. Judged against cost-to-serve: if LTV does not comfortably exceed it, the subscription loses money per pump.
What it costs to keep one subscribed pump running over the analysis horizon — support, cloud hosting, service visits. The unit-economics counterpart to LTV.
Annual Recurring Revenue — subscription revenue normalized to a yearly rate. The standard measure of the size of a subscription business.

Average Selling Price — what customers actually pay per unit after discounts, as opposed to list price. If hardware ASP falls as subscriptions rise, the subscription may be quietly funded by hardware discounts ("cannibalization").
Of the devices in the field that could carry the companion subscription, the share that actually do. The core adoption measure for software sold on top of hardware.

questions.question: What is our actual share of the US PCA/smart-pump segment — taking share from BD/Baxter or growing with the market?
questions.verdict_headline: US (NA-proxy) PCA/LVP smart-pump share is a RANGE, not a number: ~0.029%–0.047% of installed base and ~0.55%–1.1% of annual segment dollars (A-003 denominator, LOW confidence); our installed base grew ~16.0%/yr vs the assumed market ~7.3%/yr — directionally gaining, from a tiny base (mismatched bases: ours is UNIT growth of our NA in-segment book; A-003's rate is the DOLLAR CAGR of the total US infusion-pump market — directional comparison only)

question.what: A market-share estimate for the US PCA / smart-pump segment, built from our installed-base records and a stated market-size assumption — deliberately presented as a range, not a point figure.
question.why: Share tells you whether growth is winning customers from competitors or just riding market growth — but only if the estimate is honest about how soft its denominator is.

installed-units.label: Our in-segment installed base
installed-units.what: The count of our pumps in service in the segment, from our own fleet records.
installed-units.why: This is the hard half of the share calculation — the numerator we actually measure, independent of any market-size assumption.

share-range.what: Our estimated share expressed as a range, produced by dividing our measured installed base by a market-size assumption recorded as an assumption record.
share-range.why: The denominator is assumed, not measured, so a single share number would overstate precision; the range width is an honest display of that uncertainty.
share-range.how_to_read: Treat the whole range as the answer. Narrowing it requires better market-size data, not more computation.

units-by-line.what: Our in-segment installed base split by product line.
units-by-line.why: It shows which products actually carry our market presence, and where the installed base that future subscriptions attach to sits.

share-trend.what: The share range tracked across fiscal years, holding the market-size assumption constant.
share-trend.why: With a constant denominator, movement in this trend reflects our own installed base growth — the part of the share story the data actually supports.

growth-rate.what: Our installed-base growth rate next to the assumed growth rate of the market.
growth-rate.why: Growing slower than the market means losing share even while unit counts rise — the comparison catches that quiet failure mode.
growth-rate.how_to_read: If our bar is below the market's, we are diluting even as we grow.

competitor-unit-split.what: Competitor installed-unit counts (the major incumbents' fleets) — data no public source provides, so the gap is stated instead of estimated.
competitor-unit-split.why: Without competitor unit counts, share can only be computed against an assumed market total; this names the missing data that would harden the estimate.

verdict.what: The verdict deliberately reports share as a range and labels its confidence, because the denominator rests on a recorded assumption rather than measured market data.
verdict.why: A precise-looking share number would be false comfort; the range communicates both the position and the quality of the evidence behind it.

questions.question: Are we winning displaced accounts where an incumbent has an open recall or integration disruption — and how long does the window stay open?
questions.verdict_headline: Method demo (fabricated CRM joined to REAL FDA recall dates): we win 67.3% of decided opportunities where the incumbent had an FRN recall posted within 180 days of close (n=55) vs 14.3% outside the window (n=7); there is no uniform decay across the interior buckets (65.8% → 70.6% → 0.0%); the >12 months / no prior recall tail sits at 50.0% (n=2)

question.what: A displacement analysis: do we win more often when the incumbent vendor at an account has a recent public recall, and how long does that window of opportunity stay open? Built by joining our sales log to real FDA recall dates.
question.why: Competitor disruptions are the cheapest sales openings that exist. Knowing whether we actually convert them — and how fast the advantage decays — tells sales where to aim first.

inwindow-rate.label: In-window win rate
inwindow-rate.what: Our win rate on decided deals where the incumbent vendor had a public recall posted within the disruption window before the deal closed.
inwindow-rate.why: This is the direct measure of whether we capitalize on competitor trouble — compared against our win rate everywhere else.

window-split.what: Win rate inside the disruption window next to win rate outside it.
window-split.why: The gap between the two bars is the size of the displacement effect; no gap would mean recalls are not actually converting into wins.
window-split.how_to_read: A higher in-window bar supports targeting recently disrupted accounts.

window-sensitivity.what: The same split recomputed with a shorter disruption window.
window-sensitivity.why: If the effect only appears under one window choice, it is fragile; if it holds under both, the finding is robust to the definition.

decay-buckets.what: Win rate bucketed by how many months have passed since the incumbent's most recent recall.
decay-buckets.why: The decay shape says how perishable the opening is — how quickly sales must engage a disrupted account before the advantage fades.

recalls-by-incumbent.what: Public FDA recall counts for the infusion-pump category, per competitor firm.
recalls-by-incumbent.why: It shows where disruption windows have been opening — which incumbents' customer bases have been experiencing recall churn.

quarterly-outcomes.what: Decided deal outcomes per quarter, split into in-window and out-of-window deals.
quarterly-outcomes.why: It shows how much of our deal flow actually touches a disruption window — context for how much revenue the displacement play can realistically drive.

verdict.what: The verdict is explicitly a METHOD DEMONSTRATION: the FDA recall dates are real, but the sales records they are joined to are fabricated demo data. The pattern shows how the analysis works, not a real conversion result.
verdict.why: Rerun against the real sales log, this same method yields a decision-grade answer on where displacement selling pays; until then the numbers illustrate mechanics only.

questions.question: Where do we sit vs Alaris/Spectrum IQ/Plum 360 on 5-year TCO per pump — the buyer's spreadsheet?
questions.verdict_headline: Indicative, assumption-bounded: our 5-yr TCO is $8,900/pump all-in ($5,100 on the capital+service basis) vs a class-wide competitor range of ~$3,000–$15,000 on capital+service ONLY — competitor consumables and software subscription are undisclosed and excluded, so their true all-in TCO sits ABOVE that range; the ranges overlap and no hard we-win claim is supportable

question.what: A total-cost-of-ownership comparison: what one of our pumps costs a hospital over the ownership horizon (hardware, software, consumables, service) against the range for competitor pumps — on a stated, like-for-like basis.
question.why: Hospital buying committees decide on the multi-year cost spreadsheet, not the sticker price. Knowing where we land in that spreadsheet — and how solid the comparison is — shapes pricing and deal strategy.

our-tco.label: Our TCO per pump
our-tco.what: Our pump's ownership cost over the horizon, stated two ways: all-in (every cost stream) and on the narrower basis competitor figures actually cover, so the comparison is like-for-like.
our-tco.why: Quoting only the all-in figure against competitors' narrower figures would make us look artificially expensive; the dual basis keeps the comparison honest.

tco-comparison.what: Our pump against the class-wide competitor cost range on the comparable basis. Competitor figures rest on a recorded pricing assumption, not published price lists.
tco-comparison.why: This is the buyer's-eye view of our price position — with the range and the assumption flag communicating how soft the competitor side of the ledger is.
tco-comparison.how_to_read: Position within the range matters less than the basis note: the comparison excludes cost streams competitor data does not cover.

our-tco-components.what: Our ownership cost broken into its parts — capital, software subscription, consumables, service.
our-tco-components.why: The component mix shows which lever moves our competitive cost position most, and how much of the cost arrives as recurring streams after purchase.

feature-context.what: The competitor feature-comparison cells behind this analysis, each labeled with its verification status.
feature-context.why: Cost comparisons only mean something between comparable products; this shows what capability accompanies each price point and which cells are verified versus vendor-claimed.

tco-history.what: Our cost position tracked over time — history that accumulates only as the analysis is recomputed against refreshed competitor data.
tco-history.why: Competitor pricing moves; a position that erodes across refreshes is the signal to watch. The gap is stated until the history exists.

verdict.what: The verdict is labeled indicative and assumption-bounded: competitor costs rest on a recorded pricing assumption, and the comparable basis omits cost streams competitor data does not report.
verdict.why: It supports directional pricing conversations, not deal-level price setting — using it beyond that would lend borrowed precision to an assumed number.

terms.definition: Total Cost of Ownership — everything a buyer pays over an ownership period: purchase price plus consumables, software, and service. Hospital buying committees compare pumps on TCO, not sticker price — it is the buyer's spreadsheet.

terms.definition: Dose Error Reduction System — the safety software in a "smart" infusion pump that checks each programmed dose against a hospital-configured drug library and warns or blocks when the entry is outside safe limits.

Measuring the carbon dioxide in a patient's exhaled breath — a fast, direct indicator that breathing is slowing. It matters for PCA pumps because opioid overdose suppresses breathing; a pump integrated with capnography can pause dosing when breathing deteriorates.

candidates.what: The top and bottom of the composite ranking: the feature the evidence most supports accelerating, and the feature it least supports keeping, with their scores.
candidates.why: These two names are the analysis's output — the specific portfolio moves the underlying evidence points at.

composite.what: Every eligible feature's composite score, combining the evidence axes by the method committed in the analysis plan.
composite.why: Seeing the whole ranking — not just the extremes — shows how far apart the candidates really are and which features sit in the undecided middle.

robustness.what: How the two candidate picks behave when the scoring weights are perturbed — whether the same names keep surfacing.
robustness.why: A pick that survives weight changes reflects the evidence; a pick that flips with the weights reflects the formula. Only the first kind should drive a decision.

attach-rate.what: The subscription attach actual used as the demand axis for cloud-delivered features.

noncloud-demand.what: A demand signal for the features that do not ride the cloud platform — an evidence stream the current data does not carry, so the gap is stated.

verdict.what: The verdict names the pull-forward and kill candidates but is explicitly decision support, not the decision — the composite is a structured reading of imperfect evidence streams, with known gaps.

The standard FDA review route for most moderate-risk devices. The maker shows its new device is as safe and effective as a similar device already legally on the market, and FDA "clears" it for sale. FDA sorts every type of medical device into a short letter code (a "product code"). All of FDA's public databases — clearances, recalls, adverse-event reports — are indexed by these codes, so pulling every record for one code is how you look at a whole device category at once.

questions.question: How does our adverse-event profile compare to competitors — and what denominator did you use, because MAUDE doesn't have one?

question.what: A comparison of adverse-event report volumes across infusion-pump manufacturers from FDA's public MAUDE database — with an explicit account of why report COUNTS can be compared but event RATES cannot.
question.why: "How does our safety profile compare?" is a fair executive question with a trap inside: public data has no per-manufacturer count of devices in use, so any rate comparison would be built on an invented denominator.

total-events.label: Class-wide event volume

monthly-events.what: Class-wide adverse-event reports per month for the infusion-pump category — all manufacturers combined.
monthly-events.why: The category's monthly rhythm gives the baseline against which any one manufacturer's shift would be judged, and shows category-level changes worth knowing about on their own.

events-by-mfr.what: MAUDE adverse-event report counts per manufacturer, with name variants merged under a versioned alias map.
events-by-mfr.why: Counts show the scale of each manufacturer's report volume — but a bigger installed base produces more reports at the same underlying safety level, so counts alone must not be read as relative safety.
events-by-mfr.how_to_read: Read as report volume, never as a safety ranking — the fleet-size denominator that would make it one does not exist in public data.

rate-by-mfr.what: Events per installed device per manufacturer — the chart everyone wants, shown as a stated gap because the denominator (each manufacturer's fleet size) is not public.
rate-by-mfr.why: Publishing the gap, rather than a rate built on a guessed denominator, is the analysis's core honesty move; the gap names exactly what data (a defensible installed-base assumption) would unlock the comparison.

verdict.what: The verdict splits the question in two: report counts are comparable with caveats, while the rate comparison is BLOCKED until the installed-base assumption record is quantified.
verdict.why: Declaring the blockage is the deliverable — it prevents a plausible-looking but indefensible safety comparison from reaching a board slide.

questions.question: Any field signal — complaints, near-misses, alarm data — around opioid over-delivery or PCA-by-proxy?
questions.verdict_headline: WATCH TRIGGERED on our internal log (demo-fabricated): 3 over-delivery and 2 PCA-by-proxy-suspected complaint records (2 MDR-filed, 1 under investigation) — E-20.1 zero-tolerance NOT met; the signal→upgrade loop closed for 2 watch-category signals; real class-wide MAUDE context is counts-only (no denominator)

question.what: A standing watch on the franchise's nightmare scenarios: any internal field signal — complaints, near-misses, open regulatory items — around opioid over-delivery or PCA-by-proxy, set against class-wide public adverse-event volumes for PCA pumps.
question.why: Over-delivery is the harm a PCA pump exists to prevent; even one confirmed event carries outsized clinical, regulatory, and franchise consequences. This watch exists so the first signal is seen in a dashboard, not in a regulator's letter.

watch-stat.label: Watch-category events (internal log)
watch-stat.what: The count of complaint records in the watched categories — over-delivery and suspected PCA-by-proxy — on our internal log.
watch-stat.why: Against a zero-tolerance expectation, any non-zero count here is the headline; these are the events that escalate directly to clinical leadership.

watch-events.what: The watch-category events broken out by category.
watch-events.why: Over-delivery and PCA-by-proxy have different mechanisms and different mitigations — the split says which failure mode is actually appearing.

watch-monthly.why: Timing reveals clustering — events bunched around a firmware version or campaign period point at a common cause.

watch-signals.what: The watch-category entries in the field-signal register, with their dispositions.
watch-signals.why: A watch event that never reached a disposition is a process failure layered on a safety signal — this tracks whether each signal was actually run to ground.

docket-watch.what: Open regulatory-docket items (such as filed MDRs) in the watched categories.
docket-watch.why: It connects the internal safety signal to its regulatory reporting posture — what FDA has been told, and what is still open.

class-monthly-events.what: Class-wide adverse-event reports per month for PCA pumps from FDA's public MAUDE database — all manufacturers, not just us.
class-monthly-events.why: The class-wide rhythm is context: it shows the background level of reported harm in this device category and any category-level shifts worth knowing about.

total-class-events.label: Class-wide event volume
total-class-events.what: The total public adverse-event report volume for the PCA pump class over the charted period, with the most recent months excluded because reports arrive with a delay.
total-class-events.why: It sizes the category's overall reported-harm background — the environment any single manufacturer's signal sits inside.

class-event-rate.what: The PCA-class event rate per installed device — unavailable for the same reason as every MAUDE rate: no public denominator exists.
class-event-rate.why: The stated gap guards against reading class volumes as class risk rates.

alarm-data-gap.what: Event-level alarm analytics from the device fleet — a telemetry stream the current data does not carry, stated as a gap.
alarm-data-gap.why: Alarm data is where a near-miss shows up before a complaint does; naming the gap is the case for building that pipeline.

verdict.what: The verdict fires when any watch-category event appears on the internal log — a zero-tolerance trigger — and reports the reporting posture of each event. The internal log is demo-fabricated; the class-wide MAUDE volumes are real.
verdict.why: A zero-tolerance watch only works if a single event visibly trips it; the verdict is designed to be impossible to miss rather than proportionate to volume.

terms.definition: Patient-Controlled Analgesia — pain-medication (typically opioid) infusion where the patient presses a button to receive a dose, within programmed safety limits. The device class of our lead product, PP3500.

Someone other than the patient — a family member or caregiver — pressing the PCA dose button. It defeats the built-in safeguard that a patient sedated by the drug cannot press for more, and is a recognized cause of opioid over-delivery.

FDA's public database of adverse-event reports about medical devices. questions.question: Do we have the capacity to execute the remaining waves on schedule — or do we add headcount, contract labor, or slip?

question.what: The campaign capacity question: given each region's current completion pace and what remains, can existing field capacity finish the waves by the close date — or is the real choice between adding capacity, converting work to remote, and slipping the date?
question.why: "Work harder" is not a plan. Quantifying the gap between required and actual pace turns the capacity decision into arithmetic leadership can act on.

capacity-stat.label: Remaining campaign load
capacity-stat.what: The devices still to update, and how many of those sit in regions whose progress has stalled.
capacity-stat.why: Remaining load in a moving region is schedule; remaining load in a stalled region is a problem — the split is the point.

weekly-trend.why: The observed pace each region can actually sustain — the evidence base under every projection in this analysis.

required-rate.what: Each region's current weekly pace next to the pace required to finish by the close date.
required-rate.why: The gap between the paired bars is the capacity shortfall, region by region — the analysis's central comparison.
required-rate.how_to_read: Where the required bar exceeds the current bar, that region misses the date without intervention.

anchor-sensitivity.what: The same run-rates recomputed under an alternative anchor for "current pace" (measuring from the latest completion instead of the data date).
anchor-sensitivity.why: Stalled regions make rate arithmetic sensitive to where you anchor "now"; showing both keeps the stall from being averaged away.

remote-convertible.what: Of the devices still needing on-site visits, how many could be handled remotely because the device is connected.
remote-convertible.why: Remote conversion is the cheapest capacity lever available — it removes site visits without adding headcount.

fse-days-remaining.what: The remaining on-site workload converted into field-service days — a floor based on productive labor time, excluding travel.
fse-days-remaining.why: Workload in days is the unit staffing decisions are made in; the floor framing says the true need is at least this much.

fse-capacity.what: The field-service side of the equation — roster size and utilization — which the current data does not carry, stated as a gap.
fse-capacity.why: Workload without capacity is half a plan; the gap names the dataset needed to finish the staffing math.

verdict.what: The verdict names the capacity gap per region — stalled, behind, or on track against the required pace — and sizes the remote-conversion lever.

expectations.what: The yardstick: existing capacity absorbs the remaining waves without surge or slip. Marked unvalidated — implicit in the wave plan and never checked against an actual field-service roster.
expectations.why: A capacity assumption nobody validated is a schedule risk wearing a plan's clothes; the flag keeps that visible.

question.what: The fleet software-currency census: what share of the installed fleet runs outdated firmware, how far behind, where, and whether connected devices stay more current than unconnected ones.
question.why: Every device behind on firmware runs without the newest fixes — and each version left behind makes the eventual catch-up campaign bigger. Fleet currency is the standing measure of that accumulating debt.

behind-stat.label: Fleet currency
behind-stat.what: The share of the fleet at least one firmware version behind current.
behind-stat.why: The single number that says how much of the field is running old software — and how large the update debt has grown.

currency-history.what: Fleet currency tracked over time — history that accumulates as this census is recomputed across fleet snapshots.
currency-history.why: One reading cannot say if currency is improving or decaying; the stated gap will fill as successive snapshots accrue.

behind-by-region.what: The share of devices behind, per region.
behind-by-region.why: Regional concentration says where the next update campaign's work actually is.

currency-by-connectivity.what: The share of devices on the current version, split by connected versus unconnected.
currency-by-connectivity.why: Connectivity's promise is cheap remote updates; if connected devices are no more current than unconnected ones, that promise is not being collected on.
currency-by-connectivity.how_to_read: A small or absent gap between the two bars means connectivity is not yet translating into fleet currency.

questions.question: Is the Cloud Suite attach-rate stage-gate holding — the gate that releases the $24M predictive-monitoring spend?
questions.verdict_headline: The attach stage-gate HOLDS at the stand-in level: 43.0% of the PP3500 installed base (295 of 686 pumps) vs the 40% gate — but the $24M releases on a gate NUMBER nobody has ratified; the strategy of record says 'traction' and sets no threshold — and the verdict is denominator-definition-sensitive: under a whole-PCA denominator (884 pumps incl. 198 unconnectable PP3000) attach reads 33.4%, BELOW the stand-in gate; the metric definition is as unratified as the gate number

question.what: The stage-gate check: the flagship fleet's subscription attach rate against the gate level that releases the next major investment — including how the rate moves under alternative denominator choices.
question.why: The gate exists so a large spend follows demonstrated demand rather than hope. This is the standing measurement of whether that demonstration has happened.

attach-stat.label: Attach rate
attach-stat.what: The share of the flagship installed base under an active subscription.
attach-stat.why: This is the gate metric itself — the adoption evidence the investment decision is conditioned on.
attach-stat.how_to_read: Compare against the gate level — noting that the gate number itself is a stand-in nobody has ratified.

denominator-sensitivity.what: The attach rate recomputed under alternative denominator choices (which devices count as the eligible base).
denominator-sensitivity.why: A gate decision that flips with the denominator definition is not a robust decision; this shows how much the verdict depends on that choice.

cumulative-attach.what: Pumps under currently-active subscriptions, over time.
cumulative-attach.why: The build curve shows momentum toward the gate — and whether progress is recent or stalled.

attach-breakdown.what: The installed base split by subscription segment (active, lapsed, never subscribed).
attach-breakdown.why: Lapsed and never-subscribed pools need different plays (win-back versus first sale); the split sizes each.

attach-by-region.why: Regional spread shows whether adoption is a broad pattern or one strong region carrying the average.

gap-sites.what: Sites whose pumps are connected but not subscribed.
gap-sites.why: The named conversion targets — hardware-ready customers where attach can be won without any install work.

attach-history.what: The attach rate over time — a history that requires successive fleet-and- subscription snapshots to build, stated as a gap until they accumulate.
attach-history.why: Gate decisions should read a trajectory, not a single point; the gap names what is needed to provide one.

verdict.what: The verdict tests attach against the gate level and — just as important — flags that the gate number itself is a stand-in: strategy conditions the spend on demonstrated traction but never ratified a figure.
verdict.why: A gate that no one formally set can release a major spend by default; the verdict surfaces the unratified number as its own finding.

expectations.what: The yardstick: attach reaches the gate level before the gated spend releases. Marked unvalidated — the numeric gate is a stand-in for a strategy commitment that names no number.
expectations.why: Ratifying the gate number is the real decision this analysis keeps pointing back to.

terms.definition: Of the devices in the field that could carry the companion subscription, the share that actually do. The core adoption measure for software sold on top of hardware.

questions.question: What's our fully-loaded cost per update, remote vs on-site — and the business case for a remote-first campaign at the top non-connected accounts?
questions.verdict_headline: A remote update costs $120 vs an on-site update between $193 (labor-time floor) and $950 (full-day ceiling) — remote is 12.6–62.1% of on-site depending on unmeasured travel; a $380 adapter pays back in 0.5–5.2 update campaigns at the top non-connected accounts

question.what: The update-economics analysis: what one completed update actually costs by method (remote versus on-site), and the investment case for equipping the largest unconnected accounts with connectivity so future campaigns run remotely.
question.why: The cost gap between a remote session and a truck roll is the economic engine behind the connectivity strategy; this analysis prices that gap and the payback of closing it.

cost-per-update.label: Cost per completed update
cost-per-update.what: The cost of one completed update by each method — remote at the session rate, on-site at a labor-time floor that excludes travel and overhead.
cost-per-update.why: The per-unit cost gap, multiplied across a campaign, is the money at stake in the method mix.
cost-per-update.how_to_read: The on-site figure is a floor; the true fully-loaded gap is wider than shown.

weekly-by-method.what: Completed updates per week, split by method.
weekly-by-method.why: The realized method mix — whether the campaign is actually shifting toward the cheaper channel or just could.

onsite-cost-bounds.what: The on-site cost per update as an envelope, from the labor-time floor to a full-day ceiling.
onsite-cost-bounds.why: Without measured travel time, the honest answer is a range; decisions should survive both ends of it.

method-connectivity.what: Completions cross-tabulated by method and device connectivity.
method-connectivity.why: Connected devices updated on-site are money left on the table — this finds the mismatch between what the fleet allows and how the work was done.

adapter-case.what: For the largest unconnected accounts: the one-time cost of connectivity hardware against the recurring on-site cost each campaign incurs there.
adapter-case.why: This is the remote-first business case at the account level — capital once versus truck rolls forever.

adapter-payback.what: How many update campaigns it takes for an account's connectivity hardware to pay for itself.
adapter-payback.why: Payback in campaigns is the deciding unit: short paybacks make conversion near-automatic; long ones confine it to strategic accounts.
adapter-payback.how_to_read: Fewer campaigns is a faster payback — those accounts convert first.

finish-current-campaign.what: The projected cost of completing the current campaign's remaining on-site backlog.
finish-current-campaign.why: The near-term number: what the remaining truck rolls will cost if nothing is converted before the campaign ends.

fully-loaded-onsite.what: The true fully-loaded on-site cost per update — including measured travel, scheduling overhead, and repeat visits — which current data cannot support, stated as a gap.
fully-loaded-onsite.why: Everything here prices on-site work at a floor; the missing time-and-motion data would replace the envelope with a number.

terms.definition: Field Service Engineer — a technician who travels to customer sites to install, service, and update devices. FSE days are the scarce capacity behind every on-site campaign; anything that avoids a site visit frees them.

A cost figure that counts everything actually consumed — labor time, travel, overhead — not just the obvious out-of-pocket expense. Used so a "cheap" activity is not undercosted by ignoring the labor behind it.
